Week 6 Overview

The Purpose of This Week

Weeks 1–5 built your TOGAF knowledge from the ground up:

  • Week 1: TOGAF structure, ADM overview, 4 domains, core terminology
  • Week 2: ADM Phases A–E — objectives, steps, inputs, outputs
  • Week 3: Preliminary Phase, Phases F–H, Governance, Techniques, Content Framework
  • Week 4: Enterprise Continuum, TRM/III-RM, Views/Viewpoints, Content Framework (full), Synthesis
  • Week 5: Applied domain deep dives, cross-domain cascade, TOGAF + complementary frameworks

Week 6 has a different purpose: consolidation and exam preparation. You are not learning major new material. You are:

  1. Filling the remaining gaps — topics that need deeper treatment before the exam
  2. Synthesizing across weeks — building the connections that only become visible once you know everything
  3. Building master reference tables — the consolidated exam-ready summaries you will use in Week 7–8 practice
  4. Learning exam technique — how to read TOGAF scenario questions; how to eliminate wrong answers; how to manage 60 minutes for 40 questions
  5. Testing yourself — the final 40-question pre-mock quiz that mirrors the real exam's weight distribution

Topics That Need Final Deep Treatment

The following topics were introduced across Weeks 1–5 but benefit from one more focused pass before the exam:

Topic Where Introduced Why Another Pass

Exam Weight Summary — What the Final Exam Tests

The TOGAF 9 Associate (Level 1) exam:

  • 40 questions | 60 minutes | 60% pass score (24/40)
  • All multiple-choice, single correct answer
  • Questions are either recall (what is X?) or scenario (which concept applies here?)

Day 1 (Monday): Requirements Management, Stakeholder Management, and Architecture Capability

Section A: Requirements Management — The Center of the ADM Wheel

What Requirements Management Is

Requirements Management is the continuous process at the center of the TOGAF ADM that manages architecture requirements throughout the entire ADM cycle. It is represented as the hub at the center of the ADM wheel diagram — because ALL phases both receive requirements from it and feed requirements back into it.

Requirements Management is NOT a phase you complete and move on from. It is an ongoing process that runs in parallel with every ADM phase from Preliminary through Phase H.

The Formal Purpose

Requirements Management ensures that all architecture requirements — business requirements, architecture requirements, constraints, and principles — are identified, stored, maintained, and fed into the relevant ADM phases at the right time.

What Requirements Management Does

Requirements Management performs four functions throughout the ADM:

1. Identifies requirements — As each phase proceeds, new requirements are discovered. Phase A discovers stakeholder concerns. Phase B discovers capability gaps. Phase C discovers data quality requirements. Phase D discovers infrastructure requirements. All are captured by Requirements Management.

2. Stores requirements — Requirements are stored in the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS), which is a living document updated throughout the ADM cycle.

3. Assesses impact of change — When a new requirement arrives or an existing requirement changes, Requirements Management assesses its impact on the current architecture work and flags phases that may need to revisit their work.

4. Prioritizes and validates — Not all requirements can be fully satisfied simultaneously. Requirements Management helps prioritize between competing requirements and validates that requirements are consistent with Architecture Principles.

Requirements Management and the ADM Phases

Every ADM phase has a two-way relationship with Requirements Management:

Requirements Management
          ↕
Preliminary ↕  Phase A ↕  Phase B ↕  Phase C ↕  Phase D ↕  Phase E ↕  Phase F ↕  Phase G ↕  Phase H
  • INTO each phase: Requirements Management provides the current set of relevant requirements as input
  • OUT of each phase: Each phase returns updated, refined, or new requirements back to Requirements Management

This bidirectional flow is what makes Requirements Management the "hub" — it ensures that requirements discovered in Phase B (business) can influence Phase C (data and application) and Phase D (technology) without having to restart the ADM cycle.

Types of Requirements in TOGAF

Requirement Type Description Example
Business Requirements What the business needs the architecture to enable "The organization must be able to process payments 24/7"
Architecture Requirements Specific requirements for the architecture itself "All external APIs must conform to OAuth 2.0"
Functional Requirements What specific functions the system must perform "The customer portal must support self-service account management"
Non-Functional Requirements Quality attributes the system must exhibit "Response time must be < 2 seconds for 95th percentile"
Constraints Fixed limits within which the architecture must operate "Budget is capped at $2M"; "Must use existing data center infrastructure"
Assumptions Conditions assumed to be true for the architecture to work "The legacy CRM will be decommissioned by Q4 2027"

Where Requirements Are Stored

Requirements are stored in the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) — a formal deliverable produced in Phase A and updated throughout the ADM cycle. The ARS is:

  • A LIVING document — it is updated in every phase as new requirements are discovered
  • An INPUT to Phase B, C, D — each domain design phase reads the ARS to understand what requirements the architecture must satisfy
  • A BASELINE for compliance — Phase G Compliance Assessments measure the delivered system against the ARS

Exam tip: Requirements Management is the CENTER of the ADM wheel — not a phase you pass through, but a continuous process running throughout. The Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) is the document that stores requirements. When a question says "an organization discovers a new non-functional requirement mid-architecture-development — what process handles this?" → Requirements Management. When it says "which document contains all architecture requirements, constraints, and non-functional requirements?" → Architecture Requirements Specification.

Section B: Stakeholder Management — Full Treatment

Why Stakeholder Management Is Architecturally Critical

TOGAF recognizes that architecture exists to serve stakeholders — not the reverse. If the architecture does not address stakeholder concerns, it will not be adopted, funded, or successful. Stakeholder Management is therefore woven through the entire ADM — but its primary work happens in Phase A.

The architecture team cannot design the right architecture without first understanding:

  • Who the stakeholders are
  • What they care about (their concerns)
  • What level of detail they need (their viewpoints)
  • How much power and influence they have over the architecture's success

The Stakeholder Management Approach in Phase A

Phase A stakeholder management follows a structured four-step approach:

Step 1: Identify Stakeholders List everyone who has an interest in the architecture or is affected by it. This is broader than most architects expect:

  • Business executives (CEO, CFO, COO)
  • IT leadership (CIO, CTO, CISO)
  • Business unit managers (heads of Finance, HR, Operations, etc.)
  • End users of the systems being designed
  • Architecture team members
  • External parties (regulators, auditors, customers, suppliers)
  • Project managers who will implement the architecture

Step 2: Classify Stakeholders Use a Stakeholder Map to classify stakeholders by their interest and influence:

HIGH INFLUENCE
       |
 KEY    |  MANAGE
PLAYERS | CLOSELY
       |
HIGH ──┼───────── LOW
INTEREST|        INTEREST
       |
 KEEP  |   MONITOR
INFORMED|
       |
LOW INFLUENCE
  • High influence, high interest: Manage closely — these stakeholders can block or champion the architecture
  • High influence, low interest: Keep satisfied — they have power; don't let them become obstacles
  • Low influence, high interest: Keep informed — they care but cannot block; good sources of detailed requirements
  • Low influence, low interest: Monitor — minimal engagement needed

Step 3: Understand Concerns For each key stakeholder, document their primary concerns — what they care about, what risks worry them, what success looks like from their perspective.

Stakeholder Example Concerns
CEO Business value, time to market, competitive positioning
CFO Cost control, ROI, budget certainty, risk of cost overrun
CIO Technical feasibility, IT governance, integration complexity, support costs
CISO Security posture, compliance, data protection
Business Unit Manager Operational continuity, process change burden, staff training
End User Usability, system availability, productivity impact
Regulator Compliance with regulations, audit trail, data residency

Step 4: Map Concerns to Viewpoints Each stakeholder concern maps to one or more Architecture Viewpoints:

  • CEO's concern with business value → Business Footprint Diagram, Value Stream Map
  • CFO's concern with costs → Business Case in Phase A, Architecture Roadmap (investment phasing)
  • CISO's concern with security → Security Architecture Viewpoint (cross-cutting)
  • End User's usability concern → System Use Case Diagram, Application/User Location Diagram

Stakeholder Management Documents in TOGAF

Document Phase Purpose
Stakeholder Map Phase A Classifies stakeholders by influence and interest
Stakeholder Register Phase A Lists all stakeholders with their concerns, classification, and communication needs
Architecture Communication Plan Phase A/F Defines when and how each stakeholder group will be communicated with
Architecture Vision Phase A output Communicates the high-level target architecture to stakeholders in accessible language
Architecture Views Phases B, C, D Tailored representations of the architecture for specific stakeholder concerns

The Stakeholder Concern → Viewpoint → View Chain (Revisited)

This chain (from Week 4) is tested directly in relation to stakeholder management:

Stakeholder has a CONCERN
         ↓
Architect selects or creates a VIEWPOINT that addresses that concern
(A viewpoint is a specification: what information to show, in what notation)
         ↓
Architect creates a VIEW by applying the viewpoint to the specific architecture
(A view is the actual diagram, table, or document produced)
         ↓
Stakeholder reviews the VIEW to have their CONCERN addressed

Exam tip: Stakeholder concerns drive architecture views. When a scenario says "a senior executive is concerned about which applications support which business capabilities" → this concern drives an Application/Business Function Matrix (the view). When it says "the security officer wants to understand data access controls" → this concern drives a Data Security Diagram (the view). Concerns → Viewpoints → Views is the chain.

Section C: Architecture Capability — The TOGAF Concept

What Architecture Capability Means in TOGAF

The term "Architecture Capability" in TOGAF has a specific meaning distinct from "Business Capability" (the strategic ability of the organization to perform something). Architecture Capability refers to the organization's own ability to practice enterprise architecture — its internal EA function.

Architecture Capability covers:

  • The people: roles, skills, team structure of the EA function
  • The processes: how EA work is done (the adapted ADM)
  • The tools: modeling tools, repository systems, governance platforms
  • The governance: the Architecture Board, review processes, compliance mechanisms
  • The culture: how well the organization accepts and uses architecture

This is what the Preliminary Phase establishes — it sets up the organization's Architecture Capability before any architecture project begins.

Architecture Capability Maturity

TOGAF recognizes that organizations are at different levels of EA maturity. A common maturity model (referenced in Part VII) has five levels:

Level Name Characteristics
0 None No EA practice; ad-hoc architecture decisions; no governance
1 Initial Some architecture activity but informal; no consistent process; depends on individuals
2 Under Development EA practice being established; some governance exists; inconsistent application
3 Defined EA process formally defined and documented; Architecture Board exists; governance applied consistently
4 Managed EA practice measured and monitored; metrics tracked; process improvements made based on data
5 Optimizing EA practice continuously improved; architecture decisions demonstrably aligned to business value; EA is a strategic asset

Architecture Capability in the Preliminary Phase

The Preliminary Phase establishes Architecture Capability by:

  1. Assessing current maturity — Where is the organization today on the maturity scale?
  2. Defining target maturity — What level does the organization want/need to reach?
  3. Creating a capability roadmap — How will the organization move from current to target maturity?
  4. Establishing governance — Architecture Board composition, roles, decision rights
  5. Staffing the EA function — Chief Architect, Architecture Board members, domain architects
  6. Selecting tools — Modeling tools, repository systems, governance workflows

Architecture Capability vs. Business Capability — The Distinction

This distinction is tested precisely because the same word ("capability") is used for two very different concepts:

Business Capability Architecture Capability
What the BUSINESS can do (e.g., "Customer Onboarding") What the EA FUNCTION can do (e.g., "run an ADM cycle")
Stable strategic ability The practice of enterprise architecture
Modeled in the Business Capability Map (Phase B) Established in the Preliminary Phase
Subject to gap analysis in Phase B Assessed using maturity models in Preliminary
Supported by applications and technology Supported by EA tools and governance

Exam tip: "Architecture Capability" in TOGAF = the organization's EA practice capability (from the Preliminary Phase). "Business Capability" = what the business can do (from Phase B). They are completely different concepts that use similar language. A scenario describing "the organization's ability to run ADM cycles, maintain an architecture repository, and operate an Architecture Board" → Architecture Capability (Preliminary Phase concept).

Key Takeaway for Day 1

Requirements Management is the continuous process at the CENTER of the ADM wheel — it runs throughout every phase, feeds requirements into each phase, and receives updated requirements from each phase. The Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) is its living output document. Stakeholder Management (primarily Phase A) follows a four-step approach: identify → classify → understand concerns → map concerns to viewpoints. The concern → viewpoint → view chain produces tailored architecture representations for specific stakeholders. Architecture Capability (Preliminary Phase) = the organization's own EA practice maturity — distinct from Business Capability (Phase B) = what the business can do.

Day 2 (Tuesday): Gap Analysis Technique, Compliance Levels, and Tailoring TOGAF

Section A: Gap Analysis — Unified Technique

What Gap Analysis Is

Gap Analysis is one of the most fundamental TOGAF techniques. It is performed in Phases B, C (Part 1 and Part 2), and D — once per architecture domain — and its results are consolidated in Phase E.

The purpose: identify the differences between the Baseline Architecture (AS-IS — current state) and the Target Architecture (TO-BE — desired future state), and classify those differences so they can be addressed in the Architecture Roadmap.

The Gap Analysis Process — Formal Steps

Gap Analysis in TOGAF follows a consistent process across all domains:

Step 1: Document the Baseline Architecture The current state of the domain is fully described — what capabilities, processes, data entities, applications, or technology components currently exist.

Step 2: Document the Target Architecture The desired future state of the domain is fully described — what should exist after the architecture is implemented.

Step 3: Compare Baseline to Target Systematically compare every element: what exists in both? What exists only in the baseline? What exists only in the target?

Step 4: Classify Each Gap Each difference is classified:

Gap Classification Meaning Example
Added Exists in Target but NOT in Baseline — must be created New "Open Banking" capability not in baseline
Eliminated Exists in Baseline but NOT in Target — must be removed Manual reconciliation process to be retired
Changed Exists in BOTH but is different in Target — must be modified Loan approval process reduced from 10 days to 24 hours
Retained (Unchanged) Exists in BOTH and is the same — no action required Core payroll function unchanged
Gap (Missing from baseline) A target requirement that has no baseline counterpart "No CDM exists; one must be created"

Step 5: Assess Gap Impact For each gap, assess: How significant is this gap? What effort is required to close it? What risks exist if it is not closed?

Step 6: Create Gap/Solution Matrix Document each gap with its classification, impact assessment, and potential solution approach. This becomes the input to Phase E where gaps become Work Package candidates.

Gap Analysis Applied Per Domain

Domain Phase Examples of Gaps Found
Business Phase B New capabilities not in baseline; roles not yet defined; processes that must change
Data Phase C Part 1 New data entities required; CDM not yet in place; data quality standards not enforced
Application Phase C Part 2 Applications to be retired (Eliminate); new applications needed; integrations to migrate from P2P to ESB
Technology Phase D EOL infrastructure to be replaced; new cloud platforms to be adopted; standards to be updated

The Gap/Solution Matrix

The Gap/Solution Matrix is a key Phase B/C/D output that feeds Phase E. It captures:

Column Content
Gap ID Unique identifier for the gap
Domain Which architecture domain (Business, Data, Application, Technology)
Gap Description What is missing or different between baseline and target
Classification Added / Eliminated / Changed / Gap
Impact High / Medium / Low; what happens if not addressed
Potential Solution High-level approach to closing the gap
Phase E Work Package The Work Package this gap maps to

Phase E — Gap Consolidation

In Phase E, the architect consolidates all the gap analyses from Phases B, C, and D into a single view across all domains. This is where cross-domain dependencies between gaps are identified:

  • A Business Architecture gap (new capability) may require an Application Architecture gap (new application) AND a Data Architecture gap (new data entity) AND a Technology Architecture gap (new cloud platform) — all linked.
  • Phase E groups related gaps into Work Packages that deliver coherent capability increments.

Exam tip: Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, D — NOT Phase E. Phase E consolidates the results. The Gap/Solution Matrix from each domain phase feeds Phase E where gaps become Work Packages. When an exam question asks "in which phase is gap analysis first performed?" → Phase B (Business Architecture). When it asks "where are gap analysis results consolidated?" → Phase E.

Section B: Compliance Levels — Full Treatment

The Six Compliance Levels

Compliance levels describe how well a project or delivered solution conforms to the architecture. They are assessed in Phase G (Implementation Governance) using Compliance Assessments. There are six levels, ordered from strongest conformance to non-conformance:

FULLY CONFORMANT
    |  (Strongest: fully implements the architecture)
CONFORMANT
    |  (Implements the architecture in the spirit and letter)
COMPLIANT
    |  (Meets stated requirements; some gaps but no conflicts)
CONSISTENT
    |  (Uses same terminology/concepts but no direct relationship)
IRRELEVANT
    |  (Architecture concerns simply do not apply)
NON-CONFORMANT
    |  (Conflicts with or violates the architecture)

Detailed definitions:

Level Definition Plain-Language Indicator
Fully Conformant The solution fully implements the architecture in every specified aspect; no deviations "This system does everything the architecture specified, exactly as specified"
Conformant The solution implements the architecture in all significant respects; minor deviations are acceptable and documented "This system meets the architecture; there are minor documented deviations that don't affect the intent"
Compliant The solution meets the stated architecture requirements but does not actively implement all aspects of the architecture "This system does what the requirements say but isn't a full architecture implementation"
Consistent The solution uses the same terminology and concepts as the architecture but has no direct relationship to it — neither implements nor conflicts "This system speaks the same language as the architecture but isn't actually connected to it"
Irrelevant The architecture's concerns are simply not applicable to this solution "This system is completely outside the scope of this architecture"
Non-conformant The solution actively conflicts with or violates the architecture; it does the opposite of what the architecture specifies "This system contradicts the architecture requirements"

When Compliance Levels Are Assessed

Compliance Assessments happen in Phase G during the implementation of projects. The architect reviews:

  • Is the delivered solution doing what the Architecture Contract required?
  • Does it use the technologies specified in the Architecture Requirements Specification?
  • Does it comply with the Architecture Principles?
  • Does it meet the performance and quality standards in the ARS?

What Happens When Non-Conformance Is Found

When a Compliance Assessment finds a Non-conformant solution, the architect has three options:

  1. Remediate: Change the solution to bring it into conformance with the architecture — implement what was required
  2. Request a Dispensation: Submit a formal Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board asking for a time-limited exception to the architecture requirement, with a remediation plan included
  3. Revise the Architecture: If the Non-conformance reveals a flaw in the architecture itself (not just the implementation), submit an Architecture Change Request to formally update the architecture — then the revised architecture becomes the standard

Exam tip: Compliance level scenarios are very common. Key patterns: "uses the same vocabulary but has no direct relationship to the architecture" → Consistent. "Conflicts with the architecture" → Non-conformant. "Meets the requirements but doesn't fully implement the architecture" → Compliant. "The architecture doesn't apply to this system" → Irrelevant. When Non-conformance is found, the options are: Remediate, Dispensation Request, or Architecture Change Request.

Section C: Tailoring TOGAF — What Can Be Customized

Why TOGAF Is Designed to Be Tailored

TOGAF is explicitly designed to be adapted for each organization's context. The Preliminary Phase is where this tailoring happens. TOGAF cannot be applied identically in a 50-person startup and a 100,000-person global bank — the framework must be scaled appropriately.

TOGAF Part I states: "TOGAF is designed to be used in conjunction with a framework of other standards and is itself designed to be adapted for use in a specific environment."

What CAN Be Tailored

Element How It Can Be Tailored Example
ADM Phase Sequence Phases can be combined, run in parallel, abbreviated, or iterated more frequently Combine Phases B and C for a small organization; run abbreviated monthly cycles for Agile
ADM Phase Scope Each phase can be scoped narrowly (just one domain) or broadly Run Phase B-only to define a new business capability without touching technology
Terminology TOGAF terms can be replaced with the organization's own equivalent terms Replace "Architecture Board" with "Technology Review Committee" if that is what the org uses
Governance Processes The Architecture Governance process can be aligned with existing governance structures Integrate with an existing Change Advisory Board; use existing project approval workflows
Deliverable Format TOGAF specifies WHAT deliverables to produce; organizations decide HOW they are formatted Use Visio instead of ArchiMate; use PowerPoint instead of formal documentation
ADM Guidelines and Techniques Organizations select which Part III techniques to use Choose to use Business Scenarios but skip the formal Capability-Based Planning if not relevant
Reference Models Organizations can use the TRM and III-RM as starting points and add to them Add cloud-specific service categories to the TRM to reflect the organization's cloud strategy

What CANNOT Be Changed (the ADM Core)

While TOGAF is highly flexible, certain core elements must be respected:

  • The logical sequence of the ADM cannot be reversed (Business before Technology — always)
  • The governance principle — significant architectural decisions must be reviewed and approved
  • The stakeholder management principle — architecture must address stakeholder concerns
  • The iterative nature — architecture is not a one-time activity

Tailoring in Practice — The Tailored Architecture Framework

The output of Preliminary Phase tailoring is the Tailored Architecture Framework — the organization's own customized version of TOGAF. It documents:

  • Which ADM phases and steps will be used
  • Which deliverables are mandatory vs. optional
  • What the governance structures look like (roles, decision rights)
  • What terminology is used
  • What tools are approved
  • Which external frameworks (ITIL, COBIT, etc.) are integrated

Exam tip: Tailoring happens in the PRELIMINARY PHASE. The output is the Tailored Architecture Framework. TOGAF cannot be used without tailoring — it is designed to be adapted. What can be tailored: phase sequence, scope, terminology, governance, deliverable format. What cannot be changed: the logical cascade (Business before Technology), governance principle, stakeholder management principle.

Key Takeaway for Day 2

Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, and D (one per domain) and consolidated in Phase E. Each gap is classified as Added, Eliminated, Changed, or Retained. The Gap/Solution Matrix feeds Phase E where gaps become Work Packages. The six compliance levels (Fully Conformant → Conformant → Compliant → Consistent → Irrelevant → Non-conformant) are assessed in Phase G. Non-conformance options: Remediate, Dispensation Request, or Architecture Change Request. Tailoring TOGAF happens in the Preliminary Phase and produces the Tailored Architecture Framework. What can be tailored: phases, scope, terminology, governance, format. What cannot: the Business → Technology cascade direction, governance principle, stakeholder management.

Day 3 (Wednesday): ADM Iteration Types and Phase Steps Comparative Review

Section A: ADM Iteration — Three Distinct Types

Why Iteration Matters

The ADM is not a one-time linear process. TOGAF explicitly supports and encourages iteration — returning to earlier phases, running the ADM at different scopes, and using the ADM continuously. Understanding the three types of iteration is tested in exam scenario questions.

Type 1: Iteration Within the ADM Cycle (Within-Cycle Iteration)

What it is: Returning to an earlier phase within the SAME architecture cycle because new information, requirements, or stakeholder feedback requires revising earlier work.

When it happens:

  • Phase B is complete. During Phase C, the data architect discovers that the business process model in Phase B was missing a critical step that creates new data — return to Phase B to update.
  • A stakeholder review in Phase D reveals that a technology constraint makes the application architecture in Phase C unworkable — return to Phase C to revise.

Why TOGAF allows this: Architecture discovery is inherently iterative. You cannot always know everything you need to know about a later phase before completing an earlier one. The ADM allows backtracking without abandoning the cycle.

What triggers it: Stakeholder review feedback, discovery of a new requirement, realization that prior work was incomplete or incorrect.

Type 2: Iteration Between ADM Cycles (Cycle Iteration)

What it is: Running the ENTIRE ADM cycle multiple times — each cycle producing an increasingly detailed or refined architecture.

Three levels at which cycle iteration happens:

Architecture Landscape Levels: TOGAF defines three landscape levels at which ADM cycles can be run:

Level Scope ADM Application
Strategic Architecture Enterprise-wide; long-term direction (3–5 years) Full ADM cycle; high-level; driven by business strategy
Segment Architecture A specific business domain, division, or program ADM cycle scoped to the segment; more detailed than Strategic
Capability Architecture Specific capability increment being delivered Most detailed; directly supports a specific project or program

In practice, a Strategic Architecture defines the broad direction. Multiple Segment Architectures implement different parts of it. Multiple Capability Architectures implement each segment in project-level detail.

Why this matters for the exam: A scenario saying "a large bank runs one ADM cycle to define its 5-year transformation direction, then a separate ADM cycle for its digital banking division, then specific ADM cycles for individual capability improvements" → This is Cycle Iteration at three landscape levels.

Type 3: Phase H Iteration (Change-Driven Iteration)

What it is: Phase H monitors the deployed architecture and triggers partial or full re-entry into the ADM when changes are needed.

Three types of change trigger different re-entry points:

Change Type Trigger ADM Re-entry
Simplification Change Minor change; does not require formal architecture update Handled within Phase H; no new ADM cycle
Incremental Change Moderate change; requires some architecture revision but not a full redesign Re-enter at Phase E or Phase F for re-planning; does not need a new Phase A
Re-architecting Change Fundamental change; requires a complete redesign Re-enter at Phase A; start a new ADM cycle

Examples:

  • A regulatory update requires adding a new data field to an existing report → Simplification Change → Phase H handles it
  • A new product launch requires adding three new applications and modifying several integrations → Incremental Change → loop back to Phase E/F
  • A merger acquisition requires redesigning the entire enterprise architecture for two combined organizations → Re-architecting Change → new Phase A cycle

Exam tip: Know all three iteration types. Scenario questions describe a situation and ask "which ADM approach applies?" The trigger words: "within the current cycle" → within-cycle iteration. "Running the ADM at the enterprise level AND division level" → cycle iteration / landscape levels. "A change after deployment" → Phase H iteration with one of three change types.

Section B: ADM Phase Steps — Consolidated Comparison

Why Phase Steps Matter for the Exam

Each ADM phase has formally defined steps. The exam tests two things:

  1. Does a candidate know that Phases B, C, and D follow the SAME 9-step pattern?
  2. Does a candidate know the EXCEPTIONS — Phase A (11 steps, different purpose) and Phase E (11 steps, consolidation purpose)?

The Standard 9-Step Pattern (Phases B, C, D)

Phases B (Business Architecture), C (Data Architecture), C (Application Architecture), and D (Technology Architecture) all follow this same general pattern:

Step Activity
Step 1 Select reference models, viewpoints, and tools
Step 2 Develop Baseline Architecture Description (AS-IS)
Step 3 Develop Target Architecture Description (TO-BE)
Step 4 Perform Gap Analysis
Step 5 Define candidate roadmap components
Step 6 Resolve impacts across the Architecture Landscape
Step 7 Conduct formal stakeholder review
Step 8 Finalize the architecture
Step 9 Create Architecture Definition Document (update)

Why this pattern is important: It encodes the fundamental logic — understand where you are (baseline), define where you need to be (target), identify the differences (gap analysis), plan the transition (roadmap components), review with stakeholders, document the result. Every domain architecture follows this same logic.

Phase A Steps (Different — 11 Steps)

Phase A has a different structure because its purpose is VISION and SPONSORSHIP, not detailed design:

Step Activity
1 Establish the architecture project
2 Identify stakeholders, concerns, and business requirements
3 Confirm and elaborate business goals, drivers, and constraints
4 Evaluate capabilities
5 Assess readiness for business transformation
6 Define scope
7 Confirm and elaborate Architecture Principles
8 Develop Architecture Vision
9 Define the Target Architecture value propositions and KPIs
10 Identify transformation risks and mitigation activities
11 Develop Statement of Architecture Work; secure approval

Day 5 (Friday): Critical Distinctions Deep Drill and Expanded Exam Traps

Section A: The 20 Most Commonly Confused TOGAF Concepts

These 20 pairs represent the most frequent sources of wrong answers in the TOGAF Level 1 exam. Read each pair, understand the distinction, and practice recalling it cold.

1. Architecture Vision vs. Architecture Definition Document (ADD)

  • Architecture Vision (Phase A): A short, high-level, aspirational description of the target architecture for this initiative — enough to get sponsorship. Does not contain detailed architectures.
  • ADD (Phases B, C, D, F): The main architecture deliverable. Contains full baseline AND target descriptions for all four domains. Updated throughout the cycle.
  • Trap: "The Architecture Vision contains the full target architecture." → Wrong. It contains a high-level aspiration. The ADD contains the full target architecture.

2. Architecture Principles vs. Architecture Requirements

  • Architecture Principles (Preliminary Phase): General rules and guidelines that govern ALL architecture decisions across all projects. Stable. Not project-specific. Example: "Data is an Asset."
  • Architecture Requirements (ARS, updated every phase): Specific requirements for a particular architecture initiative — performance targets, standards compliance, specific capabilities needed.
  • Trap: "Architecture requirements are established in the Preliminary Phase." → Wrong. Requirements are project-specific and are managed in Requirements Management, starting from Phase A.

3. Work Package vs. Project

  • Work Package (Phase E): An ARCHITECTURE-level grouping of related gap-closing activities. Produced by the architecture team. A Work Package defines WHAT needs to be done to move from current to target state.
  • Project (Project Management): A time-bounded effort with budget, team, and deliverables managed by a project manager. A Work Package becomes one or more Projects in the project management world.
  • Trap: "Work Packages are projects." → Not quite. Work Packages are architecture constructs. Projects are their implementation vehicle.

4. Transition Architecture vs. Target Architecture

  • Target Architecture: The final desired state — the TO-BE architecture when the full transformation is complete. Only one Target Architecture.
  • Transition Architecture: A stable intermediate state between current and target. Multiple Transition Architectures may exist. Each is operational — the organization runs on it — but it is temporary.
  • Trap: "The Target Architecture is the same as the final Transition Architecture." → Wrong. Target Architecture is the final goal. Transition Architectures are stepping stones toward it.

5. Segment Architecture vs. Capability Architecture

  • Segment Architecture: An architecture for a specific part of the enterprise — a business division, a domain, or a major program. Scoped within the enterprise; derived from the Strategic Architecture.
  • Capability Architecture: An architecture for a specific capability increment being delivered — the most detailed level. Directly supports a specific project.
  • Memory aid: Strategic (enterprise-wide) → Segment (division/domain) → Capability (specific increment) — three levels of the Architecture Landscape.

6. Architecture Board vs. Architecture Sponsor

  • Architecture Board: The governance body that reviews, approves, and arbitrates architecture. Made up of representatives from multiple stakeholder groups. Grants Dispensations. Approves Architecture Contracts.
  • Architecture Sponsor: The executive who champions and funds a specific architecture initiative. Signs the Statement of Architecture Work. The Architecture Board reports to the Architecture Sponsor (and up to the board of the organization).
  • Trap: "The Architecture Board approves the Statement of Architecture Work." → Wrong. The Architecture Sponsor approves the Statement of Architecture Work. The Architecture Board approves the Architecture Contracts (Phase F).

7. Architecture Compliance Review vs. Architecture Review

  • Architecture Compliance Review (Phase G): A formal assessment comparing a delivered/in-progress solution against the Architecture Contract and ARS. Produces a compliance level rating.
  • Architecture Review (Phase A, B, C, D): A stakeholder review conducted during architecture development to validate that the architecture in progress addresses stakeholder concerns. Not a compliance check — a collaborative review.
  • Trap: "Architecture reviews happen in Phase G." → Compliance Reviews happen in Phase G. Architecture reviews (stakeholder validation) happen throughout Phases A–D.

8. Foundation Architecture vs. Common Systems Architecture

  • Foundation Architecture: The most generic level — applicable to any organization. TOGAF's own TRM and III-RM are Foundation Architecture assets.
  • Common Systems Architecture: Architectures that address common problems across multiple organizations (e.g., security architecture, systems management architecture) — less generic than Foundation, more generic than Industry-specific.

9. Architecture Pattern vs. Architecture Style

  • Architecture Pattern: A reusable solution to a recurring architecture problem in a given context. Documented as a proven solution template. Example: Hub-and-Spoke integration pattern.
  • Architecture Style: A high-level structural approach that shapes how a system is organized. Example: Microservices architecture style; SOA architecture style; Event-Driven architecture style.
  • Note: TOGAF primarily uses the term "Architecture Pattern"; "Architecture Style" is more common in software architecture literature.

10. TOGAF Part III vs. TOGAF Part VII

  • Part III (ADM Guidelines and Techniques): HOW to adapt and use the ADM. Customization guidance, iteration approaches, Business Scenarios technique, Risk Management technique, Capability-Based Planning, etc.
  • Part VII (Architecture Capability Framework): HOW to establish and maintain the EA practice (Architecture Capability). Roles, governance structures, maturity models, Architecture Skills Framework.
  • Trap: "Business Scenarios technique is Part VII." → Wrong. Business Scenarios is Part III (ADM Techniques). Part VII is about governance and capability.

11. Architecture Skills Framework vs. Architecture Maturity Models

  • Architecture Skills Framework (Part VII): Defines the competencies, skills, and experience levels expected of enterprise architects.
  • Architecture Maturity Models: Models for assessing how mature an organization's EA practice is. Referenced in Part VII but not a deliverable that architects produce for their own skills.

12. Interoperability Requirements vs. Integration Requirements

  • Interoperability Requirements (Part III technique): Requirements for how different systems, components, or organizations will work together — communication protocols, data formats, service interfaces. A formal technique in TOGAF Part III.
  • Integration Requirements: Similar concept but less formally defined in TOGAF. Often used interchangeably in practice, but for the exam, know that TOGAF uses the term "Interoperability Requirements" in Part III.

13. Architecture Repository vs. Enterprise Repository

  • Architecture Repository: The TOGAF-defined six-layer repository for storing all architecture artifacts, standards, governance records, and reference models.
  • Enterprise Repository: A generic term for any organizational knowledge store. Not a TOGAF-specific term. Do not confuse with Architecture Repository.

14. Strategic Architecture vs. Enterprise Architecture

  • Strategic Architecture (one of three landscape levels): An enterprise-wide architecture at a high level of abstraction, focused on long-term direction.
  • Enterprise Architecture: The broader discipline — the practice of designing and governing the overall structure of an organization's IT and business environment. TOGAF is a framework for Enterprise Architecture.

15. Conformant vs. Compliant (Compliance Levels)

  • Conformant: The solution conforms to the architecture in all significant respects. Minor documented deviations acceptable.
  • Compliant: The solution meets the stated requirements but doesn't fully implement all aspects of the architecture. Meets requirements without implementing the full architecture intent.
  • Memory aid: Conformant > Compliant. Conformant is a stronger endorsement.

Section B: Expanded Exam Traps (15 Additional Traps Beyond Week 4)

Trap 11: "Requirements Management is Phase 0 or a separate initial phase"

  • Wrong. Requirements Management is NOT a phase — it is a continuous process represented at the CENTER of the ADM wheel. It runs in parallel with every phase.

Trap 12: "Architecture Contracts are outputs of Phase A"

  • Wrong. Architecture Contracts are outputs of Phase F.
  • Phase A output: Statement of Architecture Work (governs architecture development).
  • Phase F output: Architecture Contracts (govern implementation).

Trap 13: "The Architecture Board creates the architecture"

  • Wrong. The Architecture Board GOVERNS architecture — it reviews, approves, arbitrates, and grants exceptions.
  • Architects CREATE the architecture.

Trap 14: "Phase H Architecture Change Management means making the changes"

  • Wrong. Phase H MANAGES change — it evaluates change requests, classifies them, and decides whether to absorb them (Simplification), loop back to E/F (Incremental), or start a new cycle (Re-architecting).
  • The actual CHANGES are made in the ADM phase that Phase H redirects to.

Trap 15: "Transition Architectures are produced in Phase F"

  • Wrong. Transition Architectures are IDENTIFIED and DEFINED in Phase E.
  • Phase F USES Transition Architectures as inputs when creating detailed migration plans.

Trap 16: "The TRM prescribes specific technology products"

  • Wrong. The TRM provides a TAXONOMY of technology service categories — it does not specify which products to use.
  • Organizations use the TRM as a starting point to create their own Technology Reference Architecture (TRA) with specific products.

Trap 17: "Data Architecture produces physical data models"

  • Wrong. Phase C Data Architecture produces LOGICAL data models (technology-independent).
  • Physical data models are created during implementation at the project level.

Trap 18: "The Architecture Vision is the first output of Phase B"

  • Wrong. Architecture Vision is a Phase A output.
  • Phase B starts with Architecture Vision as an INPUT and produces the Business Architecture.

Trap 19: "There is a fixed set of required Architecture Viewpoints in TOGAF"

  • Wrong. TOGAF does NOT prescribe mandatory viewpoints.
  • Organizations develop viewpoints appropriate to their stakeholders and context.

Trap 20: "COBIT replaces TOGAF for organizations that need governance"

  • Wrong. COBIT and TOGAF are COMPLEMENTARY. TOGAF provides the architecture method; COBIT provides governance controls and audit mechanisms. Many organizations use both together.

Trap 21: "The Solutions Continuum contains reference architectures"

  • Wrong. Reference ARCHITECTURES are in the Architecture Continuum.
  • The Solutions Continuum contains reference SOLUTIONS (products, implementations, systems).

Trap 22: "Phase G produces the Architecture Roadmap"

  • Wrong. The Architecture Roadmap is produced in Phase E (v0.1) and finalized in Phase F.
  • Phase G uses the Architecture Roadmap (and Contracts) as inputs to govern implementation.

Trap 23: "Architecture Debt is managed in Phase E"

  • Wrong. Architecture Debt is managed in Phase H (Architecture Change Management), where it is tracked, prioritized, and remediated through the change management process.

Trap 24: "Business Capability Maps show business processes"

  • Wrong. Business Capability Maps show CAPABILITIES (what the organization can do, at a strategic level).
  • Business Processes show HOW activities are performed step-by-step (BPMN diagrams).

Trap 25: "ITIL's Change Management controls architecture change"

  • Partially wrong. ITIL Change Management controls changes to PRODUCTION IT systems.
  • TOGAF Phase H manages ARCHITECTURE change.
  • They are connected (a TOGAF architecture change that affects production must also go through ITIL Change Management) but they are different processes serving different purposes.

Exam format:

Section B: How to Read Recall Questions

Recall questions test your knowledge of TOGAF definitions, phase assignments, and document structures. They are the more straightforward question type.

The structure of a recall question:

  • Question asks for a specific TOGAF term, phase, or definition
  • Wrong answers are plausible-sounding alternatives or near-synonyms
  • Correct answer is the exact TOGAF definition or term

Strategy for recall questions:

  1. Before reading the options: What is the answer? Think of it first — before the options anchor your thinking
  2. Match your answer to an option — if your answer matches an option, select it
  3. If unsure: Eliminate options you know are wrong first, then choose between remaining options
  4. Watch for degree words: "BEST describes," "MOST accurately," "PRIMARY purpose" — these signal that multiple options may be partially correct; you need the strongest one
  5. Watch for negatives: "NOT," "EXCEPT," "CANNOT" — these reverse the logic; the wrong answers become the right answer

Section C: How to Read Scenario Questions

Scenario questions are harder because they describe a real-world situation in plain language — without using TOGAF terminology in the problem description. Your job is to identify which TOGAF concept is operating.

The four-step scenario approach:

Step 1: Read the scenario once, ignoring the question Get the story clear in your head. What situation is described? Who is involved? What is happening?

Step 2: Identify the TOGAF context Ask: Which domain? Which phase? What activity? What concept?

  • If it describes "where things are now vs. where they need to be" → Gap Analysis
  • If it describes "a change after go-live" → Phase H
  • If it describes "a delivered system that doesn't meet a specification" → Compliance Assessment / Non-conformant
  • If it describes "setting up the EA practice for the first time" → Preliminary Phase
  • If it describes "something that must be done before any architecture project starts" → Preliminary Phase
  • If it describes "a stakeholder who wants to see a specific view of the architecture" → Viewpoint / View
  • If it describes "applications in a portfolio that need rationalization" → TIME Model
  • If it describes "too many integration connections" → ESB / Hub-and-Spoke

Step 3: Read the question and identify what is being asked The question may ask for: a phase, a concept name, an artifact type, a governance action, a framework, or a recommended action.

Step 4: Scan the options — eliminate wrong answers first

  • Eliminate obviously wrong options (wrong phase, wrong concept)
  • For remaining options, find which one most precisely matches your identified concept
  • When two options are close, pick the MORE SPECIFIC one — TOGAF exam answers reward precision

Scenario question red flags (common traps in options):

  • "Phase G" as an answer for "where are contracts created" → Wrong (Phase F creates contracts)
  • "Phase A" as an answer for "where are principles established" → Partially right (they are confirmed in Phase A, but ESTABLISHED in Preliminary Phase)
  • "Architecture Board" as an answer for "who creates the architecture" → Wrong (Board governs; architects create)
  • "Transition Architecture" when the question asks about "Target Architecture" → Wrong (Transition = intermediate stepping stone; Target = final destination)

Section D: Elimination Strategy

When you are not sure of the answer, systematic elimination reduces 4 options to 2, dramatically improving your odds.

Round 1 elimination — wrong category: Identify options that are clearly wrong type:

  • If the question is about a DOCUMENT, eliminate any option that is not a document
  • If the question is about a PHASE, eliminate options naming artifacts or concepts
  • If the question is about a TECHNIQUE, eliminate governance or structural elements

Round 2 elimination — wrong phase: If remaining options name the right type of thing but different phases, eliminate the wrong phases using your phase knowledge.

Round 3 elimination — degree of fit: Between two remaining candidates, ask: which one is the MOST direct answer? TOGAF questions want the most specific, most precise answer — not a vaguely correct general answer.

When genuinely stuck:

  • Never leave a question blank — there is no negative marking
  • Guess from your remaining 2 options
  • Your intuition after 5 weeks of study is better than random
  • Move on; don't spend more than 3 minutes on any single question

Section E: Time Management for 60 Minutes

Target pace: 90 seconds per question on average.

Recommended time allocation:

Activity Time
Reading each question (first pass — no sticking) 60 seconds per question × 40 = 40 minutes
Flagged questions (return to harder ones) 15 minutes
Buffer and final review 5 minutes

Two-pass strategy:

  • Pass 1 (40 minutes): Go through all 40 questions. Answer everything you know confidently. For unsure questions, make a best guess AND flag the question for review. This ensures all 40 questions have an answer — you will not run out of time with blank answers.
  • Pass 2 (15 minutes): Return to flagged questions. With fresh eyes and the rest of the exam answered, some flagged questions become clearer. Revise if you are now more confident.
  • Final 5 minutes: Quick check — any obviously wrong selections? Any blanks?

Danger signs during the exam:

  • If you have spent 4+ minutes on a single question → guess and move on
  • If you are on question 20 and 35 minutes have passed → normal pace
  • If you are on question 20 and 50 minutes have passed → speed up significantly; use 30-second answers for the remaining 20

Mental state management:

  • If you see a question you are unsure about → do not panic; flag it, make a best guess, move on
  • If you get a question you feel confident is wrong for all options → re-read the question carefully; look for "NOT" or "EXCEPT"
  • If the exam is going well → trust your preparation; don't second-guess correct answers

Use the 4-step scenario approach (read scenario → identify TOGAF context → read question → eliminate wrong answers).
