40-Question Pre-Mock Quiz

Instructions: 55 minutes. No notes. All 40 questions must be answered. Target: 32/40 (80%).

Q1. Which part of TOGAF 9.2 contains the Architecture Development Method?

A) Part I (Introduction)
B) Part II (Architecture Development Method)
C) Part III (ADM Guidelines and Techniques)
D) Part VII (Architecture Capability Framework)

Answer: B — Part II contains the ADM — the step-by-step process for developing enterprise architectures. It is the most tested part of TOGAF (~60% of exam questions). Part I = terminology. Part III = how to adapt the ADM. Part VII = governance and EA practice.

Q2. In the TOGAF ADM, Requirements Management is described as:

A) A discrete phase that runs between Phase A and Phase B
B) The activity performed only during Phase A to capture initial requirements
C) A continuous process at the center of the ADM wheel that runs in parallel with every phase
D) A technique in Part III used for managing project-level requirements

Answer: C — Requirements Management is the continuous process at the CENTER of the ADM wheel — not a phase, not a technique. It runs throughout all phases, feeding requirements into each phase and receiving updated requirements from each phase. It is represented as the hub of the ADM wheel diagram.

Q3. An organization is beginning its first enterprise architecture initiative. Before any architecture project starts, the team is: defining architecture governance, establishing architecture principles, selecting modeling tools, adapting the TOGAF ADM to the organization's existing culture and terminology, and setting up the Architecture Board. Which ADM phase is this?

A) Phase A — Architecture Vision
B) Phase B — Business Architecture
C) The Preliminary Phase
D) Requirements Management

Answer: C — The Preliminary Phase: setting up the EA capability (governance, principles, tailoring TOGAF, tools, Architecture Board) BEFORE any specific architecture project begins. Phase A starts a specific project. Phase B designs business architecture. Requirements Management is continuous.

Q4. What is the PRIMARY purpose of the Architecture Vision produced in Phase A?

A) To provide a detailed design of the target Business, Data, Application, and Technology architecture
B) To provide a high-level, aspirational description of the target capabilities for this specific architecture initiative — sufficient to obtain sponsorship and approval to proceed
C) To produce the Statement of Architecture Work
D) To define the Architecture Principles for the ADM cycle

Answer: B — Architecture Vision = high-level, aspirational, enough to get sponsorship and approval. It does NOT contain detailed domain architectures — those are produced in Phases B, C, D. The Architecture Definition Document (ADD) contains detailed architectures. The SoAW is a separate Phase A output. Architecture Principles come from the Preliminary Phase.

Q5. (Scenario) A large bank has completed Phase A. In Phase B, the architect discovers that the business case requires a new "Digital Identity Verification" capability that does not exist today. The architect also finds that an existing manual identity verification process should be retired once the digital capability is operational. The architect documents both findings. What technique is being applied, and what are the two gap types?

A) Business Scenario technique; Added gap and Eliminated gap
B) Gap Analysis; Added gap (new capability must be created) and Eliminated gap (manual process to be retired)
C) Risk Management; High risk and Low risk
D) Capability-Based Planning; New capability and Retired capability

Answer: B — Gap Analysis: the architect is comparing Baseline to Target Architecture and identifying differences. "Does not exist today but must exist in target" = Added gap. "Exists today but must not exist in target" = Eliminated gap. Both are Gap Analysis classifications.

Q6. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the relationship between Phase E and Phase F?

A) Phase E creates Architecture Contracts; Phase F creates the Architecture Roadmap
B) Phase E identifies Transition Architectures and produces Architecture Roadmap v0.1; Phase F finalizes the Architecture Roadmap and creates Architecture Contracts
C) Phase E and Phase F are identical in purpose; Phase F merely confirms Phase E outputs
D) Phase F identifies Work Packages; Phase E uses them to create Architecture Contracts

Answer: B — Phase E = WHAT to do: consolidates gap analyses, identifies Work Packages, defines Transition Architectures, creates Architecture Roadmap v0.1 and Implementation Plan v0.1. Phase F = HOW to do it: finalizes the Roadmap, finalizes the Implementation Plan, creates Architecture Contracts. A is completely reversed.

Q7. A Compliance Assessment in Phase G finds that a delivered system uses a proprietary authentication method instead of the OAuth 2.0 standard specified in the Architecture Contract. The implementation team explains that OAuth 2.0 implementation was deprioritized due to schedule pressure. The non-conformance is real. What are the architect's options?

A) Accept the situation; schedule pressure is a valid reason for non-conformance
B) Cancel the project and restart
C) (1) Require the team to implement OAuth 2.0 to bring the system into conformance; or (2) submit a Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board with a time-bound remediation plan; or (3) if the standard itself is found to be wrong, submit an Architecture Change Request
D) Escalate to the project manager as a project management issue

Answer: C — Three options for Non-conformant findings: Remediate (implement what was required), Dispensation Request (formal exception to the Architecture Board with deadline), or Architecture Change Request (if the architecture standard itself is wrong — not appropriate here since it's an implementation failure, not an architecture flaw). Schedule pressure alone is not a valid reason — it is the basis for a Dispensation Request with remediation commitment.

Q8. (Scenario) After a new CRM system has been in production for 8 months, the sales team reports performance issues. The architecture team investigates and finds the root cause is an architectural flaw — the application was designed without connection pooling, causing database exhaustion under load. This architectural flaw will affect multiple future projects if not corrected. Which TOGAF phase manages this?

A) Phase G — Compliance Assessment
B) Phase F — update the Architecture Contract
C) Phase H — Architecture Change Management; the architectural flaw is a trigger for change
D) Phase A — start a new architecture project

Answer: C — Phase H Architecture Change Management: this is a post-deployment architectural issue that has been discovered in production. The operational problem (performance) has revealed an architectural root cause (design flaw). Phase H evaluates the change — given that it affects multiple future projects, this is likely an Incremental Change (loop to Phase E/F to redesign the connection architecture) rather than a Simplification Change. Phase G monitors during implementation; Phase H monitors after deployment.

Q9. The Architecture Repository contains six layers. Which layer stores Architecture Decision Records, Compliance Assessment reports, and Dispensation Request approvals?

A) Layer 3 — Architecture Landscape
B) Layer 4 — Standards Information Base
C) Layer 5 — Reference Library
D) Layer 6 — Governance Log

Answer: D — Layer 6, Governance Log: the complete audit trail of all architecture governance decisions — ADRs, Compliance Assessments, Dispensations, Architecture Change Requests, meeting minutes. Layer 3 stores actual architectures. Layer 4 stores standards (Mandatory/Recommended/Emerging/Retiring). Layer 5 stores reference models and reusable patterns.

Q10. (Scenario) An architect is explaining the Enterprise Continuum to a new team member. She says: "On one end, we have architectures that apply to any organization in any industry. On the other end, we have architectures that are completely specific to our organization and our context. In between are architectures that apply to all organizations with similar types of systems, and architectures specific to our industry." Which level of the Architecture Continuum corresponds to "applies to any organization in any industry"?

A) Organization-Specific Architecture
B) Industry Architecture
C) Common Systems Architecture
D) Foundation Architecture

Answer: D — Foundation Architecture: the most generic level, applicable to any organization in any industry. TOGAF's own TRM and III-RM are Foundation Architecture assets. Common Systems = patterns for organizations with similar system types. Industry = industry-specific. Organization-Specific = this specific organization only.

Q11. What is the fundamental difference between the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum?

A) The Architecture Continuum goes from generic to specific; the Solutions Continuum goes from specific to generic
B) The Architecture Continuum contains architecture designs and blueprints; the Solutions Continuum contains implementations — products, systems, and services
C) The Architecture Continuum is for technical architecture; the Solutions Continuum is for business architecture
D) They are identical in content and exist as two names for the same thing

Answer: B — Architecture Continuum = designs and blueprints (HOW to architect). Solutions Continuum = implementations, products, and systems (WHAT to implement). Both run from most generic to most specific in parallel. An architect working at the Industry Architecture level (Architecture Continuum) should source solutions from Industry Solutions (Solutions Continuum).

Q12. (Scenario) A stakeholder review in Phase D reveals that the CIO is concerned about the total cost of cloud infrastructure and wants to understand which applications run on which cloud platforms and at what monthly cost. The architect must create an architecture view to address this concern. What is the correct chain of activities?

A) Create a data model first, then create a view
B) The CIO's concern identifies the need for a specific Viewpoint; the architect selects or creates the Viewpoint (specifying what information to show and how); then applies the Viewpoint to the specific architecture to create the View
C) Create a view first, then determine if it addresses the concern
D) The Architecture Board defines all viewpoints; the architect just creates views

Answer: B — The correct chain: Concern (CIO's cost concern) → Viewpoint (specification: show applications + cloud platforms + monthly cost) → View (the actual Application/Technology Matrix or Deployment Diagram created for this architecture). The architect creates or selects the viewpoint, then creates the view. TOGAF does not mandate the Architecture Board to define all viewpoints.

Q13. Which statement BEST describes an Architecture Building Block (ABB) vs. a Solution Building Block (SBB)?

A) ABBs are used in Phase G; SBBs are used in Phase A
B) An ABB is a conceptual, technology-independent specification of what is needed; an SBB is a concrete, technology-specific implementation of an ABB
C) ABBs are purchased from vendors; SBBs are developed internally
D) They are equivalent terms used at different organizational levels

Answer: B — ABB = conceptual and technology-independent ("what is needed" — e.g., "Payment Processing Service"). SBB = concrete and technology-specific ("what implements it" — e.g., "Stripe Payment API v3"). ABBs are defined in Phases B–D (design). SBBs are identified or built in Phases E–G (implementation). A is wrong (reversed).

Q14. (Scenario) During a Business Capability Map review, a business analyst asks: "Why is 'Customer Relationship Management' shown as a single box on the Capability Map, even though it involves hundreds of processes and thousands of daily activities?" How should the architect respond?

A) "The Capability Map is incomplete; we should add all the processes"
B) "Business Capabilities describe WHAT the organization can do at a strategic level — stable, long-term, technology-independent. Processes describe HOW it is done. A Capability Map shows capabilities, not processes. The processes are documented separately in BPMN diagrams."
C) "Capabilities and processes are the same thing; the map just simplifies"
D) "The Capability Map is a Technology Architecture artifact; processes are Business Architecture"

Answer: B — Business Capability Map = WHAT (strategic, stable). BPMN Process Diagrams = HOW (operational, sequential). They operate at different levels of abstraction and are different artifact types. A Capability Map shows the strategic capabilities; BPMN diagrams document the specific processes that exercise those capabilities.

Q15. In the Business Motivation Model, which of the following represents a MEANS (not an End)?

A) Vision
B) Goal
C) Objective
D) Strategy

Answer: D — Strategy is a MEANS (Mission → Strategy → Tactic). Vision, Goal, and Objective are all ENDS (Vision → Goal → Objective). Means = how the organization achieves its Ends. Ends = what the organization is trying to achieve.

Q16. (Scenario) A data analyst reports: "The same product, 'Executive Chair Model 500,' is recorded in the ERP as 'Exec Chair 500' and in the e-commerce system as 'Executive Chair 500 Series.' Both records are for the same physical product, but the names are different." Which data quality dimension is violated?

A) Accuracy — the product name is wrong
B) Uniqueness — there are two records for the same product
C) Completeness — the product record is missing fields
D) Consistency — the same data appears differently across two systems

Answer: D — Consistency: the same real-world entity (the chair) is represented differently in two systems. The data is not wrong (both names describe the same chair) but it is inconsistent. Uniqueness would mean two separate records exist with the same or different IDs for the same entity — here both systems have their own record, which COULD also be a Uniqueness issue, but the scenario specifically describes the naming inconsistency → Consistency violation.

Q17. Which MDM implementation style provides a central store that holds ONLY cross-reference identifiers between operational systems, without storing the actual master data?

A) Centralized Style — all master data in the central store
B) Coexistence Style — both central and operational stores are authoritative
C) Consolidation Style — periodic extraction to a central read-only store
D) Registry Style — central store holds only cross-references; operational systems retain all data and authority

Answer: D — Registry Style: the central "registry" stores only ID mappings (cross-references) — not the actual data. Operational systems retain their own data and authority. This is the least invasive MDM style, requiring no changes to operational systems.

Q18. (Scenario) An organization has 20 enterprise systems. Currently there are 190 point-to-point integrations (20×19/2). Adding a new system requires 20 new integrations. The architecture team recommends an ESB. After migration: how many integrations will the 20 systems need? How many integrations will a new 21st system need?

A) 190 integrations for 20 systems; 20 new for the 21st
B) 20 integrations for 20 systems; 1 new for the 21st
C) 40 integrations for 20 systems (bidirectional); 2 new for the 21st
D) 10 integrations for 20 systems; 1 new for the 21st

Answer: B — With ESB: each system connects to the hub only. 20 systems = 20 integrations (N). Adding the 21st system requires only 1 new integration (to the hub). This is the mathematical proof of ESB's value — N connections instead of N×(N-1)/2.

Q19. (Scenario) An organization's core banking system processes all deposits and withdrawals. It is the most critical system in the enterprise. Any downtime, even for seconds, results in regulatory reporting failures and significant financial loss. The system must survive the failure of any individual server without any service interruption, and it must also survive the complete loss of the primary data center. What combination of patterns does this require?

A) Active-Passive HA + Cold Standby DR
B) Active-Active HA + Hot Standby DR
C) Active-Passive HA + Warm Standby DR
D) No redundancy needed; use daily backups

Answer: B — Active-Active HA: server failures cause no interruption (all servers serve simultaneously; load redistributes). Hot Standby DR: data center failure is recovered in minutes with a real-time synchronized replica — needed given regulatory obligations and financial impact of any downtime. Active-Passive would have brief failover time (violates "no service interruption"). Cold/Warm Standby would have hours/days RTO (unacceptable for core banking).

Q20. An organization's Architecture Board has classified "Kubernetes container orchestration" as approved for use on new development projects while a 12-month evaluation is conducted. Existing projects must continue using the current VM-based standard. Which Technology Standard category does Kubernetes have?

A) Mandatory
B) Recommended
C) Emerging
D) Retiring

Answer: C — Emerging: approved for limited/experimental use (new projects only) while being evaluated by the Architecture Board. Not yet proven at enterprise scale. Mandatory = must use. Recommended = should use. Retiring = phase out existing use.

Q21. (Scenario) An architect is conducting a Phase D Technology Architecture review and must decide between two database options: (A) PostgreSQL 16, rated Mandatory in the Technology Standards Catalog, or (B) a new distributed SQL database the development team prefers, which has no rating in the Technology Standards Catalog. The development team argues the new database offers better performance for their use case. What is the correct TOGAF-aligned decision?

A) Use the new database; performance requirements override standards
B) Use PostgreSQL 16 (Mandatory standard); if the new database is to be considered, submit it for Architecture Board evaluation as an Emerging standard candidate
C) The decision is purely a project team decision; architecture standards don't apply to database choices
D) Use whichever is cheaper; cost is the primary factor

Answer: B — PostgreSQL 16 is Mandatory — must be used. If the team wants to use a non-listed technology, the correct process is to submit it to the Architecture Board for evaluation, which may result in it being classified as Emerging (approved for pilot use). Bypassing mandatory standards without Architecture Board approval creates Non-conformance.

Q22. Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies where Transition Architectures are first defined in the ADM?

A) Phase D — as part of the Technology Architecture design
B) Phase E — when consolidating gap analyses and identifying how to sequence the transition from Baseline to Target
C) Phase F — when creating detailed migration plans
D) Phase H — when a change request triggers a new architecture development

Answer: B — Transition Architectures are DEFINED in Phase E. Phase E is the phase that identifies the intermediate stable states between the current (Baseline) and desired (Target) architecture. Phase F uses Transition Architectures as inputs for detailed migration planning — it does not create them.

Q23. (Scenario) A global consulting firm uses TOGAF for its enterprise architecture practice. In addition, it uses ITIL for managing its IT services. During a system upgrade project, the TOGAF Phase G Compliance Assessment confirms the upgraded system meets all Architecture Contract requirements. Before the upgrade goes live in production, the IT operations team says it must go through their formal approval process first. Which framework governs the production deployment approval?

A) TOGAF Phase G — the Compliance Assessment approval is sufficient
B) ITIL Change Management — all changes to production systems require CAB approval regardless of architecture compliance status
C) COBIT — all IT decisions require COBIT governance
D) The Architecture Board — it must re-approve after Phase G

Answer: B — ITIL Change Management: all changes to production systems go through the Change Advisory Board (CAB) process. This is independent of TOGAF — Phase G confirms architectural compliance, but ITIL Change Management controls production deployment risk. Both are required; they serve different purposes.

Q24. What is the TOGAF term for the formal process by which the Architecture Board grants a time-limited exception to an architecture requirement, allowing a non-conformant solution to remain in place temporarily while a remediation plan is executed?

A) Architecture Waiver
B) Compliance Acknowledgment
C) Dispensation
D) Architecture Variance

Answer: C — Dispensation: the formal TOGAF term for a time-limited exception granted by the Architecture Board. It requires a remediation plan with a deadline. A Dispensation that expires without remediation becomes Architecture Debt. "Waiver" and "Variance" are not TOGAF terms (they are used in other frameworks, which is why they appear as traps).

Q25. (Scenario) An organization has just completed a full 5-year Strategic Architecture for the whole enterprise. Now it needs to develop a more detailed architecture for its newly formed Digital Banking division, which will operate within the Strategic Architecture's constraints but needs its own architecture that addresses division-specific requirements. What type of architecture is being developed for the Digital Banking division?

A) Foundation Architecture
B) Segment Architecture
C) Capability Architecture
D) Industry Architecture

Answer: B — Segment Architecture: a more detailed architecture for a specific part of the enterprise (a division, domain, or program) that operates within the constraints of the Strategic Architecture. Foundation Architecture = most generic level (any organization). Capability Architecture = most specific level (one capability increment). Industry Architecture = part of the Enterprise Continuum, not an ADM level.

Q26. (Scenario) A Business Architect is documenting which departments are responsible for which business functions. She discovers that both the Finance department and the Operations department independently perform "Vendor Payment Authorization" — a classic separation-of-duties risk. Which Business Architecture artifact makes this visible?

A) Organizational Map — shows the reporting structure
B) Business Process Diagram — shows how the authorization is performed
C) Business Function/Organization Matrix — shows which organizational units perform which business functions, making duplication and separation-of-duties risks visible
D) Business Capability Map — shows strategic capabilities

Answer: C — Business Function/Organization Matrix: the specific artifact that maps Business Functions (rows) to Organizational Units (columns). When two units appear in the same function's row, it reveals duplication. When both "Authorize" and "Process" appear in the same unit's column, it reveals a separation-of-duties risk. The organizational map shows hierarchy. The process diagram shows steps. The capability map shows strategic capabilities.

Q27. Which statement BEST describes the role of Architecture Principles in the ADM?

A) Architecture Principles are produced as an output of Phase B
B) Architecture Principles are general rules and guidelines established in the Preliminary Phase that govern ALL architecture decisions across all ADM phases and projects
C) Architecture Principles are project-specific constraints added to the Architecture Requirements Specification
D) Architecture Principles are suggestions that can be overridden by project teams if needed

Answer: B — Architecture Principles: established in the Preliminary Phase; apply to ALL architecture decisions across ALL projects; are general rules not project-specific requirements. They are NOT produced in Phase B (they are confirmed/refined in Phase A but established in Preliminary). They are NOT the same as requirements (requirements are project-specific; principles are enterprise-wide). They CAN be overridden — but only with Architecture Board approval (via Dispensation), not unilaterally by project teams.

Q28. (Scenario) An organization has been using TOGAF for 3 years. It now adopts SAFe for Agile development. The Agile Release Train manager says their teams are delivering every 10 weeks and cannot wait for a 6-month ADM cycle to complete before building. An architecture consultant recommends: "The Enterprise Architecture team should stay 2 Program Increments ahead of development teams, making architectural decisions before teams need them." What concept is the consultant describing?

A) Phase E Work Packages
B) Architecture Runway
C) Transition Architectures
D) Abbreviated ADM Cycle

Answer: B — Architecture Runway (SAFe concept): the EA team maintaining architectural decisions ahead of development teams, so teams always have a proven foundation to build on without waiting. The runway is "consumed" as teams implement features and must be continuously extended by EA. This concept reconciles TOGAF's planning approach with Agile's iterative delivery.

Q29. An architect is comparing TOGAF and DAMA-DMBOK for a data-intensive organization. Which statement BEST describes how these two frameworks relate?

A) TOGAF replaces DAMA-DMBOK for enterprise data architecture; there is no need for both
B) DAMA-DMBOK replaces TOGAF Phase C (Data Architecture) for data management organizations
C) TOGAF Phase C Data Architecture defines the architectural WHAT (data models, flows, quality targets); DAMA-DMBOK defines the operational HOW and WHO (data governance, quality management, stewardship practices)
D) They cover the same content from different perspectives; organizations should choose one

Answer: C — TOGAF and DAMA-DMBOK are complementary at different levels. TOGAF Phase C produces the architectural blueprint for data (what entities, what quality requirements, what flows). DAMA-DMBOK provides the operational management practices that implement and maintain that blueprint (governance roles, quality management programs, metadata management). Both are needed; neither replaces the other.

Q30. (Scenario) A new regulation requires all patient data to be processed within national borders. The organization currently processes patient data through a US-based cloud provider. The architecture team classifies this as a change trigger. It requires: updating compliance processes (Business Architecture), re-classifying which data is subject to the regulation (Data Architecture), reviewing which applications process regulated data (Application Architecture), and migrating to a nationally hosted cloud (Technology Architecture). What type of change is this in Phase H terms, and how should it be handled?

A) Simplification Change — handle within Phase H without re-entering the ADM
B) Incremental Change — the change is significant and requires re-planning; loop back to Phase E/F
C) Re-architecting Change — this is a complete redesign requiring a new Phase A cycle
D) Not a Phase H concern — regulatory compliance is handled outside the ADM

Answer: B — Incremental Change: the change affects multiple domains and requires re-planning (new or revised Work Packages for cloud migration, application review, data re-classification) but does NOT require redesigning the entire enterprise architecture. Loop back to Phase E (re-plan the roadmap with new Work Packages) or Phase F (update migration plans and Architecture Contracts). Re-architecting would be for a truly fundamental enterprise-wide restructuring.

Q31. Which of the following is NOT a valid element of the Architecture Repository's Standards Information Base (Layer 4)?

A) Mandatory technology standards approved by the Architecture Board
B) Compliance Assessment reports from Phase G
C) External standards referenced by the architecture (e.g., ISO 27001, PCI-DSS)
D) Emerging technology standards under evaluation

Answer: B — Compliance Assessment reports belong in the Governance Log (Layer 6), not the Standards Information Base (Layer 4). Layer 4 contains: technology standards (Mandatory/Recommended/Emerging/Retiring), external standards, the Technology Reference Architecture, and other standards the organization has adopted. Compliance Assessments are governance records — they go in Layer 6.

Q32. (Scenario) A project has been running for 4 months. The architecture team conducts a mid-project Compliance Assessment. The project solution uses all the required technologies from the Architecture Contract, meets all stated performance requirements in the ARS, and follows all specified integration patterns. However, the architect notices that the solution implements slightly fewer non-critical features than the Architecture Contract specified — all critical features are present. Which compliance level BEST describes this?

A) Fully Conformant
B) Conformant
C) Compliant
D) Consistent

Answer: B — Conformant: meets the architecture in all SIGNIFICANT respects; minor, documented deviations are acceptable (such as implementing slightly fewer non-critical features). Fully Conformant would require meeting every specified aspect without any deviations. Compliant would suggest meeting requirements without fully implementing the architectural intent. Consistent would imply using the same terminology with no direct architectural relationship.

Q33. In TOGAF, what is the formal name for the document produced in Phase A that defines the scope, schedule, deliverables, and budget for an architecture project — and must be approved by the Architecture Sponsor before work proceeds?

A) Architecture Contract
B) Architecture Requirements Specification
C) Statement of Architecture Work
D) Architecture Vision

Answer: C — Statement of Architecture Work (SoAW): the Phase A output that formally defines and agrees the scope, budget, schedule, and deliverables of the architecture project. Approved by the Architecture Sponsor. Different from Architecture Contract (Phase F output governing implementation). Different from Architecture Vision (high-level target description). Different from ARS (requirements document).

Q34. (Scenario) During the Week 6 quiz, an architect is asked: "Which TOGAF document is updated in every phase of the ADM from Phase A through Phase H, and serves as the primary record of both the Baseline and Target architectures for all four domains?" What is the correct answer?

A) Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS)
B) Architecture Roadmap
C) Architecture Definition Document (ADD)
D) Statement of Architecture Work

Answer: C — Architecture Definition Document (ADD): the main architecture deliverable, updated in every domain design phase (B, C, D) and finalized in Phase F. It contains baseline and target descriptions for Business, Data, Application, and Technology domains. The ARS contains requirements (also updated each phase). The Architecture Roadmap is produced in Phase E and finalized in Phase F. The SoAW is created in Phase A only.

Q35. (Scenario) An architect is explaining ADM iteration to a junior architect. She says: "After we complete a full enterprise-wide ADM cycle (Strategic Architecture), we will run a separate ADM cycle focused just on the Supply Chain division. And within THAT cycle, we will run several smaller focused cycles for specific capability improvements." What types of ADM iteration is she describing?

A) Within-cycle iteration only
B) Phase H change-driven iteration
C) Cycle iteration at Strategic Architecture, Segment Architecture, and Capability Architecture levels
D) Abbreviated ADM cycles for Agile delivery

Answer: C — Cycle iteration at three landscape levels: (1) Strategic Architecture — enterprise-wide, long-term direction; (2) Segment Architecture — the Supply Chain division, within the Strategic; (3) Capability Architecture — specific capability improvements within the segment. This is the standard TOGAF three-level hierarchy of architecture landscape and the corresponding ADM cycle iteration.

Q36. (Scenario) An organization's payroll application was classified as "Tolerate" in the TIME model three years ago. Now the vendor has announced End of Life (EOL) for the underlying database platform in 18 months. After EOL, no security patches will be issued. The payroll function remains necessary but is still not strategically differentiating. What should happen, and why?

A) Nothing — it was classified Tolerate, so keep running it as-is
B) Reclassify to Eliminate — EOL means it should be decommissioned
C) Reclassify to Migrate — EOL of the underlying platform moves it from "adequate technical health" to "poor technical health"; the function is still needed but the technology must be replaced
D) Reclassify to Invest — invest in upgrading the database platform to extend its life

Answer: C — Migrate: The EOL announcement has changed the Technical Health assessment from "adequate" to "poor" (no security patches = security risk). The Business Value remains low (payroll, not a differentiator) — but C is still correct because "Migrate" applies when function is needed AND technology is poor. The function is still needed (you cannot stop paying employees). The technology is now failing (EOL). Tolerate required adequate technical health — that condition is no longer met. Eliminate would stop the function — but payroll must continue.

Q37. (Scenario) Two organizations are merging. Organization A has been using TOGAF for 5 years with a mature Architecture Board, a well-maintained Architecture Repository, defined Architecture Principles, and proven ADM processes. Organization B has no EA practice — architecture decisions are made ad hoc by individual project managers. How would the Architecture Capability maturity of these two organizations be classified?

A) Organization A = Level 4 (Managed) or Level 5 (Optimizing); Organization B = Level 0 (None) or Level 1 (Initial)
B) Organization A = Level 1 (Initial); Organization B = Level 3 (Defined)
C) Both are at Level 3 (Defined) — the difference is irrelevant for merging
D) Architecture Capability maturity is assessed after the merger, not before

Answer: A — Organization A: mature Architecture Board, proven processes, maintained repository = Level 4 (Managed) or Level 5 (Optimizing). Organization B: no EA practice, ad-hoc decisions = Level 0 (None) or Level 1 (Initial). This distinction matters for the merger — Organization A will need to extend its Architecture Capability to absorb Organization B, establishing the Preliminary Phase foundation for the combined enterprise.

Q38. (Scenario) During Phase B, an architect interviews a CFO who says: "I need to understand how our business goals translate into specific measurable outcomes — I want to see what we're committing to achieve, by when, and how we'll measure success." Which Business Motivation Model elements should the architect focus on documenting to address this concern?

A) Vision and Mission — the highest-level strategic direction
B) Goals and Objectives — Goals give direction; Objectives provide SMART measurable targets with deadlines
C) Strategies and Tactics — these define how the organization will act
D) Influencers and Assessments — these explain the external forces driving change

Answer: B — The CFO is asking for measurable outcomes with deadlines — this is the Objective level of the BMM Ends hierarchy (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound targets supporting Goals). The CFO wants to see Goals (qualitative direction) AND Objectives (SMART commitments). Vision and Mission are too high-level. Strategies and Tactics are Means, not Ends — the CFO wants outcomes, not approaches.

Q39. Which Part of TOGAF 9.2 contains guidance on how to adapt the ADM for use in different contexts — including how to combine or abbreviate phases, how to use ADM iteration, and how to apply specific techniques like Business Scenarios and Risk Management?

A) Part I — Introduction
B) Part II — Architecture Development Method
C) Part III — ADM Guidelines and Techniques
D) Part VII — Architecture Capability Framework

Answer: C — Part III (ADM Guidelines and Techniques): contains HOW to adapt, customize, and apply the ADM in different contexts. Includes iteration guidance, phase combination/abbreviation, and specific techniques (Business Scenarios, Risk Management, Capability-Based Planning, Interoperability Requirements, Architecture Patterns). Part II contains the ADM itself (the phases). Part VII contains the Architecture Capability Framework (governance, roles, maturity).

Q40. (Scenario) At the end of 6 weeks of intensive TOGAF study, an architect reflects: "TOGAF is not just a set of phases to follow. It's an integrated framework where the method (ADM), the structure of outputs (Content Framework), the storage and classification of knowledge (Enterprise Continuum and Repository), the governance of decisions (Part VII), the adaptation guidance (Part III), the starting-point reference models (TRM, III-RM), and the common vocabulary (Part I) all work together as a system." Which statement BEST describes why this integrated view is important for the exam?

A) It is not important — exam questions only test individual phase knowledge
B) Understanding TOGAF as an integrated system enables a candidate to answer novel scenario questions where a situation spans multiple TOGAF parts — for example, a question involving a governance decision, a repository action, and a phase activity simultaneously
C) This view is only relevant for TOGAF Level 2 (Practitioner) candidates
D) This view is theoretical — exam questions only test factual recall

Answer: B — The integrated view is exactly what separates candidates who can answer hard scenario questions from those who can only answer simple recall questions. Many exam scenarios involve: a phase activity that produces a deliverable that is stored in the repository that must be governed by the Architecture Board. Without seeing TOGAF as a system, these questions are confusing. With the integrated view, they become traceable.

Week 6 New Terminology

These terms are given full treatment in Week 6 or needed for consolidation.

Term Definition
Requirements Management Continuous process at the center of the ADM wheel; manages architecture requirements throughout all phases; feeds requirements into and receives requirements from every ADM phase
Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) Living document containing all architecture requirements, constraints, NFRs, and assumptions; created in Phase A and updated every subsequent phase; baseline for Phase G compliance
Stakeholder Map Visual classification of stakeholders by influence and interest; produced in Phase A; used to determine engagement strategy
Architecture Capability The organization's own enterprise architecture practice — its maturity, processes, governance, tools, and culture for doing EA; established in the Preliminary Phase
Architecture Capability Maturity A 6-level scale (0=None through 5=Optimizing) assessing how mature an organization's EA practice is
Gap/Solution Matrix Phase B/C/D artifact documenting identified gaps with their classification (Added/Eliminated/Changed), impact, and potential solution; feeds Phase E
Gap Classification Four types: Added (in target, not in baseline), Eliminated (in baseline, not in target), Changed (in both but different), Retained (in both and same)
Compliance Level One of six levels assessing conformance to architecture: Fully Conformant → Conformant → Compliant → Consistent → Irrelevant → Non-conformant
Dispensation A formal time-limited exception to an architecture requirement granted by the Architecture Board; requires a remediation plan with deadline
Architecture Change Request A formal request to change the current approved architecture; submitted to and evaluated by the Architecture Board; triggers Phase H evaluation
Tailored Architecture Framework The organization's own customized version of TOGAF, produced in the Preliminary Phase; documents which ADM phases, deliverables, governance structures, and terminology the organization uses
Within-Cycle Iteration Returning to an earlier ADM phase within the current cycle because new information requires revision
Cycle Iteration Running full ADM cycles at multiple levels: Strategic Architecture, Segment Architecture, Capability Architecture
Strategic Architecture An enterprise-wide architecture at high level of abstraction; long-term direction (3–5 years); the broadest ADM cycle scope
Segment Architecture Architecture for a specific part of the enterprise (division, domain, major program); operates within Strategic Architecture constraints; more detailed
Capability Architecture Architecture for a specific capability increment; most detailed level; directly supports a specific project or program
Simplification Change Phase H change type: minor change that can be absorbed within Phase H without re-entering another ADM phase
Incremental Change Phase H change type: moderate change requiring re-planning; triggers loop back to Phase E or Phase F
Re-architecting Change Phase H change type: fundamental change requiring complete redesign; triggers a new Phase A cycle
Work Package An architecture-level grouping of related gap-closing activities defined in Phase E; becomes one or more projects in the project management world
Architecture Sponsor The executive who champions and funds a specific architecture initiative; approves the Statement of Architecture Work
Two-Pass Exam Strategy Exam technique: Pass 1 = answer all 40 questions at ~60 seconds each (flagging uncertain ones); Pass 2 = return to flagged questions with remaining time

What to Expect in Week 7

Week 7 begins the intensive exam simulation phase:

Monday–Tuesday (Integration): Apply all TOGAF knowledge to a real end-to-end scenario — design an architecture for a specific organization using all 9 ADM phases, all 4 domains, and key governance mechanisms. This builds the ability to see the whole ADM as a flow.

Wednesday (Practice Exam 1): Full 40-question timed exam under real exam conditions. 60 minutes. No notes. Score and analyze.

Thursday (Gap Analysis from Exam 1): For every wrong answer: identify the topic, re-read the relevant study guide section (5–10 minutes per topic), write a one-sentence summary of what you now understand. Map errors to topics — identify your 2–3 weakest areas.

Friday (Targeted Re-study): 3 hours focused only on your weakest areas from Exam 1. No new material — deepen understanding of identified gaps.

Saturday (Practice Exam 2): Full 40-question timed exam. Target: 75%+ (30/40). If you reach 75%, you are on track for the real exam.

Sunday (Gap Analysis + Rest): Score analysis for Exam 2. Identify remaining gaps. Note the difference between Week 7 Exam 1 and Exam 2 scores — the trend tells you whether your weak areas are improving.

Week 7 Target: Score 75%+ (30/40) on at least one of the two practice exams.
